ta_refined.answer:
The person who springs to mind is my cousin An, whom I have always treated like an older brother. He taught me how to build a financial model, a skill that later became central to my work. I became close to him when I had just moved from marketing into an investment role and felt completely out of my depth, so I trusted his advice rather than treating it as another generic lesson.

What sets him apart is his ability to make complicated ideas feel practical and surprisingly human. He did not just explain things; he broke them into small steps, watched my reaction and adjusted the explanation when I was clearly lost. The process was demanding, but it never felt intimidating.

I saw this firsthand when he spent a Saturday helping me repair a spreadsheet whose formulas were producing nonsense. My first response was not especially impressive, yet he stayed patient and helped me focus on the next manageable step. Once the idea clicked, the change in my confidence was immediate. That detail matters because the moment showed the quality through behaviour rather than through a collection of adjectives.

Looking back, that afternoon saved me weeks of trial and error and made me much more confident at work. The experience also changed how I support other people: I try to demonstrate, let them practise and only step in when necessary. I would jump at the chance to learn from him again because the result was useful, but the manner in which it happened was even more memorable.
